items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Opening remarks before moderated conversation, University of Texas at El Paso (Listening in 360 tour)
items.quote: I am increasingly concerned that higher interest rates could be necessary later this year to fully restore price stability and appropriately balance both sides of the Fed’s dual mandate.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is trending toward the mid-2s rather than 2 percent, activity is strong, the labor market is balanced and conditions indicate policy is not restraining the economy. She said she is increasingly concerned that rate increases could be needed later in 2026, while stressing the need for FOMC debate.
items.score_note: Open to hiking later this year and says policy is not restrictive, but no call for an immediate move. AI mention is demand-side only (AI investment boom, 'The demand is here already'), not a financing link, so ai_financing not tagged.

items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Opening remarks, 'Market Liquidity and Leverage in a Digital Age' panel, NY Fed / Chicago Booth Future of Market Liquidity and Functioning Workshop
items.quote: the FOMC could make its open market operations more efficient and effective, and support the strength of U.S. markets more generally, by centrally clearing its operations on a voluntary basis
items.summary: Panel framing remarks on Treasury market liquidity, leverage and technology. Logan argued the Fed should centrally clear its open market operations voluntarily. No comment on the rate path or the economic outlook.
items.score_note: Official remarks with no rate-path content; included for coverage. Money-market and operations topic.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks on inflation, employment and monetary policy, Dallas Fed Houston Branch (before moderated conversation)
items.quote: I currently believe modestly higher interest rates would better balance the outlook and risks for the FOMC’s maximum employment and price stability goals.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is heading toward the mid-2s, not 2 percent, the labor market is solid, and labor, consumption and financial data show policy is not restraining the economy. She said modestly higher rates are warranted now ('Better modest restriction now than severe restriction later'), with inflation risks to the upside from energy and the AI investment surge. Delivered about a week and a half before the July FOMC.
items.score_note: Explicitly says higher rates would be better now, ahead of the July meeting where she dissented for a hike. [AI link: capex demand only] she cites AI investment as an upside inflation risk, not a credit or funding issue.

items.summary: The FOMC held the target range at 3.50-3.75% by a 9-3 vote. Hammack, Kashkari and Logan voted against, preferring a 25bp increase. Quote is the FOMC statement's wording of the dissent, not Logan's own words.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Statement from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan on FOMC dissent (July 28-29 meeting)
items.quote: I would have preferred to increase interest rates by one-quarter percentage point at this week’s meeting.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is trending toward the mid-2s with upside risks, the job market is solid and perhaps strengthening, and policy is not restraining the economy. She argued that modest action in the near term would reduce the likelihood of sharper action later.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Opening remarks for moderated conversation, Voices of the Eleventh District (Dallas Fed, evening event)
items.quote: I currently estimate the target range needs to rise an additional 50 basis points or more to appropriately balance the outlook and risks for our dual mandate goals.
items.summary: Two weeks after the September 25bp hike, Logan called it an important first step and said policy has been 'offsides' and needs to become modestly restrictive. She estimated at least another 50bp is needed and noted that higher term premiums, unlike higher risk-free rates, could reduce the need to tighten.
items.score_note: Explicitly says the target range needs to rise at least another 50bp.

items.quote: Good monetary policy depends on well-executed research.
items.summary: Welcome remarks on migration research and the value of the Fed's regional structure. No comment on the rate path or the outlook.
items.score_note: Official remarks with no monetary-policy stance; included for coverage.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Remarks to Davidson College students (two days after the October 27-28 FOMC)
items.quote: It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases.
items.summary: Logan said she voted to hold at 3.75-4.00% in October and described it as skipping an increase because markets had been volatile; a skip does not change the destination. She estimated the funds rate is at least 50bp below a modestly restrictive level and said at least two more 25bp hikes are needed, followed by a pause to assess.
items.score_note: Explicit call for at least two more hikes even though she voted to hold in October. [AI link: market volatility around the technology investment outlook cited as a reason to move gradually; not a credit-event claim].
items.ai_quote: Financial markets have been volatile in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Economic and monetary policy outlook, 11th joint Dallas Fed / Kansas City Fed energy conference, Houston
items.quote: It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall.
items.summary: Logan said inflation is trending meaningfully above 2 percent, October CPI was higher than expected, and the real funds rate (78bp by her staff's estimate) is below the lowest neutral estimate. She repeated that at least two more 25bp hikes are needed and added that the pace could be faster this winter, then a pause to assess.
items.score_note: Explicit call for at least two more hikes and an open door to a faster pace. [AI link: market volatility around the technology investment outlook cited for the October skip; AI capex also described as a demand driver].
items.ai_quote: Financial markets had been volatile in the weeks before the meeting in response to news on the technology investment outlook and geopolitical developments.

items.speaker: Lorie Logan
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Operational readiness and bank funding, 'Bank Funding in the Age of Instance Finance' conference, Dallas Fed
items.quote: it is necessary to make policy more restrictive, not less.
items.summary: Mostly about liquidity tools: discount window on weekends, central clearing of Fed repo operations, readiness to lend to designated financial market utilities. On Treasury market functioning she said she does not see high or rapidly rising yields as dysfunction in themselves, prefers lending tools over purchases, and said any market-functioning purchases should be separated from the policy stance (held in a separate account and sold quickly) because policy needs to tighten.
items.score_note: Rate stance is a brief restatement of the Nov 10 speech inside a balance-sheet and money-market speech; scored +2 because she says outright that policy must become more restrictive. Main content is tools.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Aspen Ideas Festival panel 'Affordability: What's Real About What We Feel?' (moderated by Lisa Abramowicz)
items.quote: In June, I've changed that to one rate hike by the end of the year,
items.summary: Kashkari said he moved his 2026 projection from one cut (March) to one hike (June), calling it a pencil mark that depends on data. He cited supply-driven inflation from tariffs and the Strait of Hormuz plus massive data-center investment, and said he does not see an all-clear in the Middle East. Minneapolis Fed lists the event at 9:30-10:30 a.m. MT.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: CNBC Squawk Box live interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin from Aspen, Colorado
items.quote: I would rather get going now in small steps than wait till later, then we have a really entrenched inflation problem and have to raise rates aggressively.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: CBS Face the Nation interview with Margaret Brennan
items.quote: Eventually, we're going to have to do more.
items.summary: Kashkari said the Treasury market is functioning despite the rise in yields (10-year at 4.7 percent), which lets the Fed focus on the funds rate as its primary tool. He would not prejudge September but said he is not confident inflation is heading back to target soon, citing the Iran conflict and the Canada tariff standoff.

items.speaker: Neel Kashkari
items.role: President, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (2026 FOMC voter)
items.occasion: Council on Foreign Relations, C. Peter McColough Series, conversation with Steve Liesman (New York)
items.quote: I had jotted down two hikes for this year, one in September and then one later on this year.
items.summary: Kashkari said inflation is still too high at around 3 percent, and the longer the economy stays resilient the more he questions how tight policy is; he raised his neutral estimate to 3.25 percent and thinks neutral is temporarily higher because of data-center capital demand. His September dots had one more hike in 2026 and one in 2027, in pencil. He said markets are signalling policy may need to go tighter than the Fed expects, that booming financial markets do not suggest policy is tight, and that away from the zero bound the Fed should stick to the funds rate rather than the balance sheet.
items.score_note: Torn between +1 and +2: he expects more hikes, but calls the dots a snapshot in pencil and hopes for 'modest adjustments', so chose the level nearer 0. [AI link: financing/capital] he ties the neutral rate and loose financial conditions to data-center capital demand and AI bond issuance, and flags AI circular funding and private credit.

coverage_notes: Presidency: Dallas Fed leadership page still lists Lorie Logan as president and CEO; Minneapolis Fed people page lists Neel Kashkari as President and CEO (both opened 2026-11-23). No change. Dissent check from the four FOMC statements: June 17 was 12-0 (hold at 3.50-3.75%); July 29 was 9-3 with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan preferring a 25bp hike; September 16 was 12-0 (hike to 3.75-4.00%); October 28 was 10-2 with Cook and Hammack dissenting, so Logan and Kashkari both voted to hold. Dallas Fed news releases show only one dissent statement in the window (July 31); Minneapolis Fed essays likewise show only the July 31 statement. Logan: every item on the Dallas Fed speeches page from June 3 to November 13 was opened (9 texts plus the dissent release). Her public calendar shows no speaking events in August or September (Jackson Hole, Aspen, roundtables only) and the calendar page stops at September 29. The Q&A portions of the June 3 and July 16 moderated conversations were not checked separately; they belong to the same occasions as the prepared remarks. No stand-alone Logan media interview was found. Kashkari: the Minneapolis Fed lists four events in the window (June 2, June 26, September 30, November 18), all video only; June 26 and September 30 are covered through CNBC and the CFR transcript, June 2 and November 18 are in unverified.
